Intro to ML: Lecture 3 15 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling model selection The more complex our model class the better our loss: So training loss alone is not usually a good metric for model selection. Small loss does not imply generalization. Intro to ML: Lecture 3 16 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling model selection Problem: Loss alone is not informative for choosing model. For more complex models, we get smaller loss on the training data, but don’t expect to perform well on “new” data: In other words, the model does not generalize. Intro to ML: Lecture 3 17 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling model selection Solution: Directly test model on “new data”. ↭ Loss continues to decrease as model complexity grows. ↭ Performance on new data “turns around” once our model gets too complex. Minimized around degree 4. Intro to ML: Lecture 3 18 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling TRAIN-TEST PARADIGM Better approach: Evaluate model on fresh test data which was not used during training. Test/train split: ↭ Given data set (X, y),splitinto twosets (Xtrain, ytrain) and (Xtest, ytest). ↭ Train q models f (1),. .., f (q) by ﬁnding parameters which minimize the loss on (Xtrain, ytrain). ↭ Evaluate loss of each trained model on (Xtest, ytest). Sometimes you will see the term validation set instead of test set. Sometimes there will be both: use validation set for choosing the model, and test set for getting a ﬁnal performance measure. Goal: Find model f ↗ {f (1),. .., f (q)} and parameter vector ε to minimize the R(f, ε). Intro to ML: Lecture 3 31 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling model selection ↭ Train q models (f (1), ε↑ 1),. .., (f (q), ε↑ q). ↭ For each model, compute empirical risk RE(f (i), ε↑ i ) using test data. ↭ Since we assume our original dataset was drawn independently from D, so is the random test subset. No matter how our models were trained or how complex they are, RE(f (i), ε↑ i ) is an unbiased estimate of the true risk R(f (i), ε↑ i ) for every i. Can use it to distinguish between models. Intro to ML: Lecture 3 46 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval - From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling feature selection Exhaustive approach: Pick best subset of q features. Faster approach: Greedily select q features. Stepwise Regression: ↭ Forward: Step 1: pick single feature that gives lowest loss. Step k: pick feature that when combined with previous k → 1 chosen features gives lowest loss. ↭ Backward: Start with all of the features. Greedily eliminate those which have least impact on model performance. Feature selection deserves more than two slides, but we won’t go into too much more detail! Intro to ML: Lecture 3 61 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling probabilistic modeling In a Bayesian or Probabilistic approach to machine learning we always start by conjecturing a probabilistic model that could have generated our data. ↭ The model guides how we make predictions. ↭ The model typically has unknown parameters ςφ and we try to ﬁnd the most reasonable parameters based on observed data (more on this later in lecture). Unknown model parameters: ↭ p0,p1, ↭ p10,p20,. ..pn0, one for each of the n vocabulary words. ↭ p11,p21,. ..pn1, one for each of the n vocabulary words. How would you estimate these parameters? Intro to ML: Lecture 3 69 / 71 Prof. Gustavo Sandoval From Last Class Model Selection Regularization Bias and Variance probabilistic modeling parameter estimation Reasonable way to set parameters: ↭ Set p0 and p1 to the empirical fraction of not spam/spam emails. ↭ For each word i,set pi0 to the empirical probability word i appears in a non-spam email. If the word i appears in 1 of 100 of non-spam emails, set pi0 =0.01. ↭ For each word i,set pi1 to the empirical probability word i appears in a spam email. Estimating these parameters from previous data examples is the only “training” we will do.
